title: Japanese Red Pine: Ancient Red Pines You Can Visit
meta_description: Three Japanese red pines, from a shrine tree in Higashi-Hiroshima to a Gifu farmhouse marker to the sole survivor of a Seattle garden avenue.
intro: Pinus densiflora is the red pine of Japan, called akamatsu for the orange-red plates its bark breaks into higher up the trunk, brighter the further you look. Matsutake, the country's most expensive mushroom, forms almost exclusively on its roots, which is one reason old red pine groves like the one at Hongu Hachiman Shrine in Higashi-Hiroshima have been tended for centuries. In the mountains above Shokawa, a single red pine forks two metres up into three trunks reaching the same height, a shape the surveyor who recorded it compared to Neptune's trident; the marker beside it, dated 1971, still calls it Mumaya Sanbonmatsu, the name three pines for a tree that is only one. In Seattle's Kubota Garden, a Japanese immigrant gardener planted an avenue of about twenty in the 1920s; a century of storms has left exactly one standing.
